title: The language and the front end
dek: Terraform is a compiler whose intermediate representation is a dependency graph and whose back end is somebody else's process. This first part of a four-part teardown follows one terraform plan through Terraform v1.17.0's front end: a Ragel scanner with five machines, a schema-less recursive-descent parser, a decoder that runs twice, go-cty values that carry unknowns, refinements and marks, a dozen small block schemas, the init graph that now evaluates module and provider addresses, and the installer that writes the lock file.
byline: 24 October 2026 · Subject: terraform@018a99c8 (v1.17.0) · Part 1 of 4 · Read from the source; measured on this machine with no cloud credentials
description: Terraform v1.17.0 taken apart, part 1: HCL's scanner and parser, schema-driven decoding, cty values with unknowns and marks, the block schemas, directory loading, the init graph and early evaluation, and provider installation with the lock file.
og_description: Part 1 of a four-part Terraform teardown at v1.17.0 (018a99c8): the five-machine Ragel scanner, precedence as a six-row slice, decode-twice and why dynamic "lifecycle" is impossible, 512-bit numbers and eager &&/||, the 15 top-level blocks, the three-vertex init graph that evaluates const variables, and why init is never offline under the default provider source.

from the code marks a fact read from hashicorp/terraform at v1.17.0 (018a99c83c5d, 21 October 2026), cited as a path and line number from the repository root. HCL is cited at its main branch (4a347c448ee9) while Terraform v1.17.0 ships HCL v2.24.0; the code quoted here is the same at both, but line numbers in hclsyntax/parser.go above about line 370 sit 9 to 10 lower at v2.24.0, and in expression.go above 1773 sit 7 lower. go-cty is cited at an untagged clone (a918e1174fca) while Terraform pins v1.18.1. measured here marks output from the v1.17.0 binary on a 2-vCPU Linux box with the providers random 3.9.1 (and aws 6.70.0, google 8.8.0, azurerm 5.10.0 in the shared plugin cache). No cloud credentials existed and nothing was applied to a cloud; every example in this part uses only the built-in terraform provider or random. Timings depend on load and page cache and are given as single runs with that caveat. reconstruction marks a judgement I drew from those sources rather than read in one place.

This is Part 1 of 4 of Terraform, taken apart. Part 2 builds and walks the plan graph and follows providers as child processes over gRPC; Part 3 covers the state file, locks, refactoring blocks and the 1.5 to 1.17 feature arc; Part 4 builds a three-cloud project with no credentials, covers the licence and the fork, and ends with the findings register.
